entries.title: Anatomy and the wiring
entries.text: Pituitary anatomy and its hypothalamic connections Where the gland sits, and why the anterior and posterior lobes fail in completely different ways. The pituitary is about 1 cm across and weighs roughly 0.5 g . It sits at the base of the brain in the sella turcica , immediately below the optic chiasm, and hangs from the hypothalamus by a stalk that carries both blood vessels and axons . Those two things in the stalk — vessels and axons — are the whole reason the two lobes behave so differently. How the hypothalamus controls each pituitary lobe The hypothalamus connects to the anterior pituitary through hypophyseal portal veins, which carry releasing hormones. It connects to the posterior pituitary through axons, which carry vasopressin and oxytocin made in hypothalamic neurons. The anterior pituitary makes and secretes growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH, and prolactin, each acting on a target organ. The posterior pituitary makes nothing itself — it stores and releases the two hormones delivered down the axons. Hypothalamus releasing hormones · AVP · oxytocin portal veins axons Anterior pituitary adenohypophysis Posterior pituitary neurohypophysis ANTERIOR — FIVE CELL TYPES, FIVE OUTPUTS GH → liver → IGF-1 → linear growth TSH → thyroid → T4 and T3 ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol LH / FSH → gonads → sex steroids, gametes Prolactin → breast → milk production POSTERIOR — NOTHING IS MADE HERE AVP (vasopressin) → collecting duct → water reabsorbed, urine concentrated Oxytocin → uterus, breast THE POINT STUDENTS MISS AVP is synthesized in hypothalamic neurons, travels down their axons, and is merely stored and released by the posterior pituitary. So a hypothalamic lesion can cause AVP deficiency. Original diagram of the hypothalamic-pituitary anatomy and axes. The two routes out of the hypothalamus explain the clinical split: anterior lobe failure is a secretory problem in the pituitary itself, whereas posterior lobe failure can originate anywhere along the hypothalamus–stalk–posterior lobe path. Anterior lobe — histology Five functional cell types: somatotropes (GH), lactotropes (prolactin), corticotropes (ACTH), gonadotropes (FSH/LH), and thyrotropes (TSH). Posterior lobe — histology Axons, Herring bodies, and pituicytes rather than glandular cells. It stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus. Primary, secondary, tertiary — define it once and reuse it everywhere This framework applies to every axis, so it is worth over-learning. Primary : the end organ has failed — the pituitary or hypothalamic hormone is elevated while the end-organ hormone is low. Secondary : the pituitary has failed — pituitary hormone low, hypothalamic hormone elevated, end-organ hormone low. Tertiary : the hypothalamus has failed — all three low. Secondary and tertiary together are called central . Retrieve A patient has a low cortisol. What would the ACTH be in primary, secondary, and tertiary disease — and which organ is at fault in each? Primary — the adrenal cortex has failed, so ACTH is high as the pituitary tries to flog a gland that cannot respond. Secondary — the pituitary has failed, so ACTH is low and cortisol is low; CRH from the hypothalamus would be elevated. Tertiary — the hypothalamus has failed, so CRH, ACTH, and cortisol are all low. The trick that makes exam questions answerable: look at whether the upstream hormone moved in the same direction as the downstream one, or the opposite.

entries.title: The three presentations
entries.text: Three ways pituitary disease presents If you can place a disorder into one of these three boxes — and notice when it belongs in more than one — most of this topic organizes itself. Three presentations of pituitary disease Pituitary disease branches into three overlapping outcomes. Hormone excess comes from functional adenomas such as prolactinoma, growth hormone adenoma, and corticotroph adenoma. Hormone deficiency comes from hypopituitarism of any cause, including craniopharyngioma, Sheehan syndrome, apoplexy, and a large adenoma crushing the normal gland. Mass effect comes from any expanding sellar lesion, causing headache, bitemporal hemianopsia, and abnormal sella imaging. A single large adenoma frequently produces all three at once. Pituitary disease 1 · Hormone excess Functional adenoma · Prolactinoma · GH → acromegaly · ACTH → Cushing · TSH, LH/FSH (rare) Symptoms of the hormone 2 · Hormone deficiency Hypopituitarism · Craniopharyngioma · Sheehan syndrome · Apoplexy · Big adenoma crushing GH first, ACTH last 3 · Mass effect Any expanding lesion · Headache, raised ICP · Bitemporal hemianopsia · Sella abnormal on MRI · Stalk effect on prolactin Non-functioning tumors too THE THREE OVERLAP — THAT IS THE EXAM POINT One macroadenoma can secrete a hormone, crush the rest of the gland into hypopituitarism, and compress the chiasm — all at the same time. When a stem mixes an excess syndrome with visual loss, that is a macroadenoma, not two diseases. Original diagram. Use it as a triage question on every vignette: which of the three is this stem describing, and is it describing more than one? Recognize Presentation, physical findings, and characteristic patterns

entries.title: Mass effect and the chiasm
entries.text: Mass effect and the optic chiasm Why a lesion in the sella takes the outer half of each visual field, and nothing else. Three consequences of local mass effect: headache from raised intracranial pressure, an abnormal sella turcica on imaging, and visual field loss, most commonly bitemporal hemianopsia . The last one is worth understanding rather than memorizing, because the anatomy explains the exact field defect. Why a sellar mass expanding upward causes bitemporal hemianopsia Light from the temporal, or outer, half of each visual field falls on the nasal half of each retina. Nasal retinal fibers cross the midline at the optic chiasm. A pituitary mass sitting directly under the chiasm and expanding upward compresses those crossing fibers first, so vision is lost in the temporal half of each visual field — bitemporal hemianopsia. Fibers from the temporal retina, which carry the nasal field, run laterally and are spared until later. STEP 1 · THE CROSSING left eye right eye chiasm to occipital cortex sellar mass expands upward solid red = crossing nasal-retinal fibers, compressed first solid blue = uncrossed temporal fibers, spared STEP 2 · THE FIELD left field right field shaded = lost Original diagram. The chain to be able to say out loud: temporal field → nasal retina → crossing fibers → sit in the middle of the chiasm → a mass pushing up from the sella hits the middle first → both temporal fields go. "Bitemporal" describes the field that is lost, not the retina. Distinguish from A defect in one eye is a lesion of that optic nerve, in front of the chiasm. A homonymous defect — the same side of the field lost in both eyes — is a lesion behind the chiasm, in the tract or radiation. Only a lesion at the chiasm produces the bitemporal pattern.

entries.title: Hypopituitarism
entries.text: Hypopituitarism and the order hormones are lost Hypopituitarism is loss of anterior pituitary output, from any cause. Two points carry most of the exam weight: GH is deficient in most patients with hypopituitarism , and acquired hypopituitarism tends to follow a sequential order of loss. The usual sequence of anterior pituitary hormone loss Acquired hypopituitarism typically loses growth hormone first, then LH and FSH, then TSH, and ACTH last. Because growth hormone goes first, its loss foreshadows the deficits that follow. ACTH deficiency is flagged as the potentially urgent one, because loss of cortisol can be life-threatening under physiological stress. GH lost first LH / FSH gonadotropins TSH thyrotropin ACTH lost last · urgent GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH WHY GH FIRST MATTERS GH loss foreshadows the deficits still to come. Short stature in a child, or an isolated GH deficiency, warrants watching the other axes. WHY ACTH LAST IS DANGEROUS It arrives late, so it is easy to miss — and cortisol deficiency is the one that kills under stress, surgery, or illness. Treat this axis before thyroid hormone. Original diagram of the classically taught sequence. The ordering is a tendency , not a law — any individual can lose axes out of order, particularly after surgery, radiation, or apoplexy. What each anterior deficiency looks like. Note that the pituitary hormone and the end-organ hormone are both low — that is the signature of central disease. Axis lost Lab pattern Clinical picture GH ↓ GH, ↓ IGF-1 Children: short stature. Adults: a diffuse picture — visceral adiposity, low bone mass, increased cardiovascular disease, fatigue, anxiety, depression, reduced quality of life, and possibly premature death. LH / FSH ↓ LH and FSH, ↓ estrogen or testosterone Women: amenorrhea, infertility. Men: decreased libido, impotence, loss of pubic and axillary hair. In children: delayed puberty. TSH ↓ TSH, ↓ T4 and T3 Central hypothyroidism. The TSH is low or inappropriately normal — this is why TSH alone is an unreliable screen when you suspect pituitary disease. ACTH ↓ ACTH, ↓ cortisol Hypocortisolism. Note that mineralocorticoid output is largely preserved in central disease, unlike primary adrenal failure. Causes, grouped by mechanism Destruction Tumors and other mass lesions · trauma and subarachnoid hemorrhage · pituitary surgery or radiation · ischemia · pituitary apoplexy. Gliomas and craniopharyngiomas are named as the most common tumors to cause hypopituitarism. Congenital Empty sella syndrome · Rathke cleft cysts · genetic defects including PIT-1 and HESX1 mutations. Inflammation Autoimmune hypophysitis. Clinical definition Isolated GH deficiency is a defined group of conditions involving absent GH action and severe short stature.

entries.title: Structural and vascular causes
entries.text: The named structural and vascular lesions Six entities the objectives name individually. Each card opens; each one ends with a distinguishing feature worth having ready. Craniopharyngioma from Rathke pouch remnants Structural lesion Rathke pouch remnant , classically in a child with growth failure, hypopituitarism, headache, and visual-field loss from a suprasellar mass. Sheehan syndrome postpartum pituitary infarction Ischemic Anterior pituitary infarction after severe postpartum hemorrhage → failure to lactate, amenorrhea, fatigue, and other anterior hormone deficiencies. Pituitary apoplexy hemorrhage into an adenoma Neurosurgical emergency The time-sensitive one on this page Acute hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma with rapid enlargement. It causes an excruciating headache , vision changes , and hypopituitarism — and it can cause cardiovascular collapse and sudden death . It is a true neurosurgical emergency . The circulatory collapse is the acute loss of ACTH and therefore cortisol. Empty sella syndrome sella filled with CSF Structural The pituitary is shrunken or flattened and the sella then fills with cerebrospinal fluid, so on imaging the sella looks empty. The clinically important part: with a partial empty sella, pituitary function is often normal . An "empty sella" on a scan is therefore not automatically a diagnosis of hypopituitarism — it is a reason to test the axes, not to assume them. Septo-optic dysplasia and congenital hypopituitarism midline malformation Congenital Optic nerve hypoplasia + absent septum pellucidum + pituitary hormone deficiency. Midline defects or neonatal hypoglycemia should prompt evaluation for congenital hypopituitarism. Rathke cleft cyst benign remnant cyst Structural Benign Rathke pouch remnant cyst , often incidental but capable of causing anterior pituitary deficiency by local compression.

entries.title: Growth hormone deficiency
entries.text: Growth hormone deficiency The axis GH acts largely through IGF-1 , generated principally in the liver. That is why the workup measures both: GH is pulsatile and a single random level is close to uninterpretable, whereas IGF-1 integrates GH exposure over time. What suppresses GH secretion Malnutrition · illness · hyperglycemia . The last one is the mechanistic basis of the diagnostic test for GH excess . What stimulates GH secretion Deep sleep · stress · exercise · hypoglycemia · sex steroids. Again, the last one is the basis of a diagnostic test — this time for GH deficiency . Testing GH stimulation tests are used, because a low random GH proves nothing. In the insulin tolerance test , insulin is given to induce hypoglycemia; someone with adequate GH reserve raises their GH in response . Failure to rise is the abnormal result. Adult GH deficiency is not just a height problem Adults have a genuinely diverse clinical picture: visceral adiposity, low bone mass, increased cardiovascular disease, excessive tiredness, anxiety, depression, reduced quality of life , and possibly premature death. In children the presentation is dominated by short stature . Retrieve An insulin tolerance test is performed on someone with intact GH reserve. What happens to serum GH, and why is that the logic of the test? Serum GH rises . Insulin drives the glucose down; hypoglycemia is a physiological stimulus to GH secretion , so a healthy somatotroph population responds. The test works by provoking the axis rather than sampling it — which is necessary because GH is secreted in pulses and a low random value is uninformative. A failure to rise is what defines the deficiency.

entries.title: Adenomas: functional or not
entries.text: Pituitary adenomas — functional versus non-functional The single most useful split in this topic. Note that they are not opposites clinically — a functional adenoma can also be large enough to do everything a non-functional one does. Functional (hormone-secreting) Non-functional Frequency Prolactin and GH are the most common functioning types; prolactinoma is the most common functional adenoma A common pituitary-tumor category How it declares itself Symptoms of the hormone it makes, so it can be caught while small Mass effect — which means it is usually large by the time it is found Typical size at diagnosis Often a microadenoma (<1 cm), especially prolactinoma in women Usually a macroadenoma (>1 cm) Effect on the rest of the gland Can also compress and destroy neighboring parenchyma if large Destroys surrounding tissue → hypopituitarism Pathology term Named for the hormone: lactotroph, somatotroph, corticotroph, thyrotroph, gonadotroph " Null cell " adenoma — no demonstrable markers of differentiation Apoplexy risk Present, and rises with size A recognized cause of pituitary apoplexy Size vocabulary Microadenoma < 1 cm · macroadenoma > 1 cm. Larger lesions can erode the sella, compress the chiasm, and cause hypopituitarism. Pathology — the two headline findings Cellular monomorphism : a pure population of acidophils, basophils, or chromophobes, rather than the mixed population of the normal gland. Loss of the reticulin network on a reticulin (silver) stain — the normal acinar architecture breaks down. Those two together are how an adenoma is distinguished from hyperplasia. Pituitary carcinoma Extremely rare. It is distinguished from an adenoma by craniospinal or systemic metastasis , not by local invasion or microscopic appearance alone.

entries.title: Prolactin and prolactinoma
entries.text: Prolactin regulation and prolactinoma Prolactin is the odd one out: it is the only anterior pituitary hormone under tonic inhibition . Understand that one fact and four different diseases fall out of it. Tonic dopamine inhibition of prolactin The hypothalamus continuously sends dopamine down the stalk to the lactotroph, which suppresses prolactin release. This is inhibition rather than stimulation, shown as a gray dashed line ending in a bar. Anything that interrupts the dopamine signal — a stalk lesion, a dopamine receptor blocker, or a lactotroph that has escaped control — raises prolactin. A dopamine agonist restores the inhibition. Hypothalamus releases dopamine, continuously inhibition (dashed = a brake) Lactotroph anterior pituitary Prolactin → breast, and suppression of GnRH Cut the brake and prolactin rises. That single idea explains every cause in the table below. Original diagram. The gray dashed line ending in a bar is this site's convention for inhibition or a lost signal — it is used the same way on every page. Four routes to a high prolactin, and one route back down. Reading the middle column is usually enough to answer the question. Situation What happens to the dopamine brake Clinical fingerprint Physiologic Normal regulation, appropriately overridden Pregnancy, suckling or nipple stimulation, stress. Not a disease. Stalk effect Brake line cut — any suprasellar mass disturbs the hypothalamic inhibitory influence reaching the lactotroph A moderate prolactin rise from a mass that does not itself secrete prolactin. The classic trap: a non-prolactin-secreting tumor with a raised prolactin. D2-receptor antagonist drugs Brake signal blocked at the receptor Antipsychotics — phenothiazines and haloperidol among them. Galactorrhea and menstrual irregularity appearing after a new medication. Prolactinoma Lactotrophs escape control and secrete autonomously; hyperplasia also interferes with normal dopamine inhibition Prolactin concentration correlates positively with adenoma size — so a very high prolactin points here rather than to stalk effect. Dopamine agonist treatment Brake restored pharmacologically Bromocriptine or cabergoline — first-line, ahead of surgery. They restore the inhibition of prolactin release. Prolactinoma lactotroph adenoma Most common functional adenoma Mechanism Autonomous prolactin secretion from a lactotroph adenoma. Serum prolactin correlates positively with the size of the adenoma . Presentation Amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, infertility, delayed puberty. Typically ages 20–40. The diagnosis is made more readily in females , because menstrual disturbance and galactorrhea declare themselves earlier than a slowly falling libido — so men more often present late, with mass effect. Pathology Dystrophic calcification, which when extensive is called a "pituitary stone." Prolactin immunohistochemistry confirms the lineage; reticulin stain shows the loss of acinar architecture common to all adenomas. Management Medication first — bromocriptine or cabergoline, dopamine receptor agonists that restore inhibition of prolactin release. Surgery is second-line. This is unusual among pituitary tumors, where surgery is more often the primary answer. Course emphasis Two things carry most of the exam weight: prolactinoma is the most common functional adenoma , and it is the one where drugs beat surgery . Add the size–prolactin correlation and you can separate a true prolactinoma from stalk effect.

entries.title: Acromegaly and gigantism
entries.text: Growth hormone excess — acromegaly and gigantism Same hormone, same tumor, two entirely different bodies. The only variable that matters is whether the growth plates are still open. Growth hormone excess before and after epiphyseal closure A somatotroph adenoma secretes growth hormone, which stimulates IGF-1. If this happens before the epiphyseal plates close, in childhood, the result is gigantism — a generalized increase in body size with disproportionately long arms and legs. If it happens after closure, in adulthood, long bones can no longer lengthen, so the result is acromegaly — continued growth of bone and cartilage producing enlargement of the hands, feet, and face, and of organs including the heart, liver, and adrenals. Somatotroph adenoma 2nd most common functioning type ↑ GH → ↑ IGF-1 EPIPHYSEAL PLATES STILL OPEN Gigantism Childhood onset. Long bones can still lengthen, so height increases. · Generalized increase in body size · Disproportionately long arms and legs Same hormone, growing skeleton EPIPHYSEAL PLATES CLOSED Acromegaly Adult onset. Bone can no longer lengthen, so it thickens instead. · Hands, feet, face enlarge · Heart, liver, adrenals enlarge Same hormone, finished skeleton Original diagram. If a question gives you GH excess and asks which phenotype, the only thing you need from the stem is the age at onset . Acromegaly — the face and hands Protrusion of the lower jaw (prognathism) , prominent supraorbital ridges , broadening of the nose , thickening of the lips , and thickened fingers . Old photographs are genuinely diagnostic, because the change is slow enough that nobody around the patient notices. Acromegaly — the systemic cost GH excess also causes gonadal dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, arthritis, congestive heart failure , and an increased risk of cancers . The cardiovascular and metabolic burden, not the appearance, is what shortens life. Diagnosis Elevated serum GH and IGF-1 . Then the confirmatory test: failure to suppress GH in response to an oral glucose tolerance test , one of the most sensitive tests for the diagnosis. It works because hyperglycemia normally suppresses GH — a tumor ignores that. Imaging with MRI , plus bone scan. Treatment Surgery , then drug therapy: somatostatin analogs (somatostatin is GHIH, growth-hormone-inhibiting hormone) or a GH receptor antagonist . Note the contrast with prolactinoma, where medication comes first. Retrieve Why does giving oral glucose help diagnose acromegaly, and what result confirms it? Hyperglycemia normally suppresses GH secretion. Load someone with glucose and a healthy somatotroph population obediently shuts down. An autonomous somatotroph adenoma does not — so the confirmatory finding is failure of GH to suppress after the oral glucose load. It is the mirror image of the insulin tolerance test used for GH deficiency, where you provoke with hypoglycemia and look for a rise.

entries.title: Corticotroph, thyrotroph, gonadotroph
entries.text: The remaining functional adenomas Corticotroph adenoma — Cushing disease and Nelson syndrome ACTH excess Cushing disease — meaning specifically the pituitary cause of Cushing syndrome — is oversecretion of ACTH from a corticotroph adenoma, stimulating the adrenals to overproduce cortisol. On histology, corticotroph tumors show Crooke hyaline change . Nelson syndrome — follow the feedback A large, destructive corticotroph adenoma appearing after bilateral adrenalectomy performed for Cushing disease. Removing the adrenals removes the inhibitory effect of adrenal corticosteroids on the tumor, which is then free to grow. The giveaway is the combination: hypercortisolism is absent — the adrenals are gone — yet the patient has mass effect and hyperpigmentation , the latter driven by the very high ACTH. Scope The adrenal side of Cushing syndrome, including the diagnostic workup separating pituitary from adrenal from ectopic sources, belongs to a different session. This page stays at the depth this topic needs. Gonadotroph adenoma LH and FSH producing Often functionally silent Usually found in middle-aged men and women presenting with neurologic symptoms once the adenoma is large enough — which is the paradox of this tumor: it secretes hormone, but the hormone it secretes does not produce a florid syndrome, so it behaves clinically much like a non-functioning tumor. It causes decreased libido and amenorrhea in premenopausal women , and secondary gonadal hypofunction , usually through impaired LH even though FSH is the predominant secreted hormone . Histology shows pseudorosettes around vascular channels and oncocytic change. Thyrotroph adenoma TSH producing Rare — but a diagnostic trap An extremely rare cause of hyperthyroidism . It earns its place here entirely because of its lab pattern: elevated TSH and elevated T4 and T3 . Why that pattern is the whole point Every other hyperthyroid state has a suppressed TSH, because excess thyroid hormone feeds back and shuts the pituitary down. A TSH that is high while the thyroid hormones are also high means the pituitary is driving the process rather than responding to it. When you see both elevated, the lesion is upstream. Cross-reference the thyroid localizer .

entries.title: Posterior pituitary: water
entries.text: Posterior pituitary — the three water disorders One hormone, and the three ways it goes wrong: too much, not enough, or present but ignored. SIADH syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone Too much AVP Mechanism AVP excess causes reabsorption of excessive free water . Retaining water without retaining solute dilutes the serum — hence hyponatremia . Presentation Neurologic, and driven by the rate of the sodium fall: confusion, cerebral edema , and neurologic dysfunction including seizures . Diagnostic pattern ↓ serum osmolality and ↓ sodium , with ↑ urine osmolality and ↑ specific gravity . Urine output is low despite appropriate or increased hydration — the kidney is concentrating when it should be dumping water. Management Water restriction. The finding that surprises people Total body water is increased, yet peripheral edema does not develop , because blood volume stays normal — the retained water distributes across all compartments rather than pooling in the interstitium. A hyponatremic patient with pitting edema is telling you about heart, liver, or kidney failure instead. AVP deficiency (AVP-D) formerly central diabetes insipidus Not enough AVP Mechanism Deficient AVP secretion. Because AVP is made in the hypothalamus, the lesion can sit anywhere along the hypothalamus–stalk–posterior lobe path. Causes Head trauma, tumors, surgery, and inflammation of the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. Presentation Polyuria and polydipsia . Large volumes of dilute urine with low specific gravity and low urine osmolality, and a concentrated serum with a raised sodium and osmolality . Treatment Replace the missing hormone — desmopressin (DDAVP) . AVP resistance (AVP-R) formerly nephrogenic diabetes insipidus AVP present but ignored Mechanism Renal tubular unresponsiveness to circulating AVP. The hormone is there; the collecting duct will not listen. Causes Medications — lithium is the most commonly cited cause. Congenital disease from an X-linked mutation of the AVPR2 gene , which encodes the receptor. Presentation Clinically almost identical to AVP-D. Polyuria, polydipsia, dilute urine, concentrated serum. You cannot tell them apart at the bedside. So how do you separate them? By responsiveness to administered AVP and by measurement of serum AVP . That is the entire content of the next section. The danger in both AVP disorders Patients with an intact thirst mechanism and free access to water can generally compensate for the urinary losses, and look deceptively well. Remove either of those — an infant, someone with altered consciousness, a patient made nil by mouth for surgery, anyone with hypothalamic damage that also took out thirst — and they develop life-threatening dehydration . The polyuria is not the emergency; the inability to keep up with it is. Localize Using the lab pattern and the response to treatment to place the defect

entries.title: Separating the water disorders
entries.text: Water-deprivation and desmopressin interpretation Three disorders, five numbers, one maneuver that separates the two that look alike. The comparison to have automatic. Read down the "urine" rows first: SIADH is the one where the urine is inappropriately concentrated , and the two AVP disorders are the ones where it is inappropriately dilute . Finding SIADH AVP deficiency (central) AVP resistance (renal) Serum sodium Low (hyponatremia) High High Serum osmolality Low — dilute serum High — concentrated serum High — concentrated serum Urine osmolality High Low Low Urine specific gravity High Low Low Urine volume Low, despite adequate or increased hydration High, despite dehydration High, despite dehydration Serum AVP Inappropriately present Low Normal or high — the hormone is there Response to desmopressin Not a diagnostic step; would worsen the hyponatremia Urine osmolality rises substantially — the kidney can concentrate once given the hormone Little or no rise — the kidney cannot respond Underlying problem Too much AVP action Too little AVP Enough AVP, unresponsive receptor Water deprivation, then desmopressin Water deprivation: continued high-volume dilute urine confirms failure to concentrate. Desmopressin: urine osmolality rises in AVP deficiency but changes little in AVP resistance . Safety — this is a supervised test, not a bedside maneuver Water deprivation can cause dangerous dehydration and hypernatremia and must be performed under close supervision. Act Evaluation, management, and the drugs named in this topic

entries.title: Evaluation and management
entries.text: What to do about it, at the depth this topic goes to Course-relevant management only. Where the course objectives stop, this table stops. Disorder Key evaluation Management principle Prolactinoma Serum prolactin (correlates with size), MRI Dopamine agonist first — bromocriptine or cabergoline. Surgery second-line. Acromegaly / gigantism GH and IGF-1; failure to suppress GH after oral glucose; MRI; bone scan Surgery , then somatostatin analog or GH receptor antagonist . Pituitary apoplexy Recognition is the test — sudden headache, visual failure, collapse Neurosurgical emergency. Hemodynamic collapse reflects acute cortisol deficiency. Hypopituitarism Test each axis; remember the pituitary hormone is low with the end-organ hormone Replace the deficient end-organ hormones. Address the underlying lesion. SIADH Serum and urine osmolality and sodium; urine output against hydration status Water restriction. AVP deficiency Water-deprivation test; response to desmopressin; serum AVP Desmopressin (DDAVP) — replacing the missing hormone. AVP resistance Same tests; the absent response is the diagnosis Giving more hormone does not work. Address the cause — lithium is a common medication cause. Drugs named in this session Bromocriptine, cabergoline Dopamine receptor agonists. They restore the tonic inhibition of prolactin release that the disease removed — which is why they work on prolactinoma and why they are first-line ahead of surgery. Desmopressin (DDAVP) Synthetic arginine vasopressin . Both the treatment for AVP deficiency and the discriminating step in the diagnostic test — the same molecule doing two jobs. Somatostatin analogs Somatostatin is GHIH , growth-hormone-inhibiting hormone. The analogs suppress GH secretion in acromegaly when surgery is not the answer or has not been enough. Drugs that cause these problems D2-receptor antagonists (phenothiazines, haloperidol) raise prolactin. Lithium causes AVP resistance. On any endocrine vignette, read the medication list before the labs. Retrieve Practice before you leave the page

entries.title: The HPT axis
entries.text: The hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis The loop Hypothalamus releases TRH → anterior pituitary releases TSH → thyroid follicular cells release T4 (mostly) and T3 (some) → peripheral deiodinase converts T4 to T3 → T3 is the active hormone at nuclear receptors. Negative feedback closes the loop at both the hypothalamus and the pituitary. The hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid feedback loop The hypothalamus releases TRH to the anterior pituitary, which releases TSH to the thyroid, which releases T4 and some T3. Rising T4 and T3 feed back negatively on both the pituitary and the hypothalamus, shown as gray dashed inhibition lines. A break at the thyroid is primary disease and moves TSH in the opposite direction to the thyroid hormone. A break at the pituitary or hypothalamus is central disease and leaves TSH low or inappropriately normal regardless of the thyroid hormone level. Hypothalamus TRH Ant. pituitary TSH Thyroid T4 → T3 negative feedback — dashed = a brake, not a signal Break the loop at the thyroid = primary . Break it upstream = central . That one distinction answers a large share of thyroid questions. Original diagram. In primary disease the break is at the gland, so TSH moves opposite to the hormone problem. In central (secondary or tertiary) disease the break is upstream, so TSH stays low or inappropriately normal regardless of T4. What thyroid hormone actually does Brain maturation · bone maturation · linear growth · thermogenesis · myocardial contractility · hepatic maturation · skin maturation · increased catecholamine sensitivity · heart rate and blood pressure. That catecholamine line is why a hyperthyroid patient looks adrenergically revved up, and why a beta blocker helps. Primary vs central, stated plainly Primary — gland is broken. ↑TSH in hypothyroidism, ↓TSH in hyperthyroidism. Central (secondary = pituitary, tertiary = hypothalamus) — TSH is low or inappropriately normal regardless of T4. An "inappropriately normal" TSH beside a low free T4 is the finding people miss. Figure by Priya Modi, Physiology Diversified . Licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 — reproduced unmodified, with attribution, for non-commercial educational use. This is the one image on this site that is not original; everything else is drawn from scratch. What the objectives ask of you, for every disorder below Identify the underlying cause — congenital, embryologic, autoimmune, infectious, nutritional, or neoplastic. Distinguish primary from secondary from tertiary. Recognize the signs and symptoms, including newborn-screening abnormalities where relevant . Select and interpret the right laboratory, imaging, and pathologic studies. And identify the indications for fine-needle aspiration, biopsy, or surgery . entries.title: Congenital hypothyroidism
entries.text: Congenital hypothyroidism Usually detected through universal newborn screening; most cases are sporadic. Speed is the whole point T4 is essential for early brain and skeletal development, and the window does not reopen. Severe untreated congenital hypothyroidism developing in infancy or early childhood is what the older literature calls cretinism — a term now avoided clinically but still occasionally encountered in older texts. Start levothyroxine as soon as the screen flags it; do not let a confirmatory workup delay treatment. Etiology Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause : hypoplasia or aplasia, or an ectopic gland from a migration defect during embryogenesis — most commonly a lingual gland. Dyshormonogenesis : an inborn error of hormone synthesis, secretion, or metabolism. Often familial. The gland is present but works incompletely or not at all — for example an organification defect or a TSH-receptor abnormality. Imaging — and how to read it Tc-99 scan. Tissue seen in the wrong place → ectopic gland , a migration defect. A normal-looking gland in a hypothyroid infant → dyshormonogenesis , because the tissue is there but not functioning. No gland seen → aplasia or dysgenesis; follow up with ultrasound. Classic signs and symptoms Macroglossia · coarse facies · umbilical hernia · lethargy, irritability, poor feeding · poor growth and weight gain · a persistently large, open fontanel · persistent jaundice · temperature instability · delayed passage of the first stool · edema. Most affected newborns look well at birth, which is precisely why the screening programme exists. Localizing congenital hypothyroidism. Treatment is levothyroxine — synthetic T4 — in both. Pattern TSH T4 / T3 Where the defect is Primary High Low The thyroid gland itself Central (secondary or tertiary) Low or normal Low Pituitary or hypothalamus — think congenital hypopituitarism The newborn screen trap A low total T4 with a normal TSH in an otherwise well, term, normal-weight infant is usually thyroxine-binding globulin deficiency , not thyroid disease. Total T4 tracks the binding protein; the free T4 and TSH are normal , the axis is intact, and no treatment is needed. Confirm with a free T4 rather than repeating a total T4. Two other explanations to hold in mind for the same pattern are central hypothyroidism and a delayed TSH surge — the latter particularly in premature, low-birth-weight, or critically ill infants, which is why the well term infant points away from it.

entries.title: Acquired hypothyroidism
entries.text: Acquired hypothyroidism and Hashimoto thyroiditis In iodine-sufficient countries, autoimmune disease is the dominant cause. Hashimoto thyroiditis chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis Autoimmune Mechanism Multiple mechanisms acting together: cytotoxicity mediated by CD8+ and CD4+ T cells , cytokines, and antithyroid antibodies. The gland shows progressive destruction of parenchyma, Hürthle cell change, and a mononuclear (lymphoplasmacytic) infiltrate . Destruction eventually produces hypothyroidism. The long silent phase A patient can carry circulating thyroid antibodies for years — or a lifetime — before hypothyroidism develops . Antibody positivity is therefore not the same as disease, and a normal TSH today does not exclude Hashimoto tomorrow. Labs and treatment ↑TSH, ↓free T4 — the primary pattern. Confirm the autoimmune etiology with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-TG) antibodies. Imaging (ultrasound, radioactive iodine uptake) is optional, not required. Treat with levothyroxine . Myxedema — acquired hypothyroidism in older children and adults Goiter · immature body proportions · fatigue and decreased energy · increased sleep · cold intolerance · dry skin and brittle hair · constipation · pubertal delay in children . Other acquired causes to know Iodine deficiency — the common cause worldwide, no longer common in the United States · prior thyroid surgery or treatment for hyperthyroidism · radiation · medications, specifically lithium and amiodarone . Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome — the company Hashimoto keeps APS 1 : autosomal recessive, AIRE gene mutation → hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadism, vitiligo. APS 2 : autosomal dominant, multifactorial → adrenal insufficiency, Hashimoto thyroiditis , and T1DM . The clinical habit worth building: one autoimmune endocrinopathy is a reason to keep an eye on the others. Cross-reference T1DM . Retrieve Someone has a high TSH and a low free T4. Which single test best establishes Hashimoto thyroiditis as the cause, and why not the others? Anti-TPO antibody. The TSH and free T4 have already localized the problem to the gland; the remaining question is why , and anti-TPO answers it serologically. TSI is the Graves antibody — wrong direction of disease. A radioactive iodine uptake scan belongs to the hyperthyroid workup, where it separates Graves from a toxic nodule from thyroiditis. Free T3 tells you about severity, not etiology, and is often not even ordered.

entries.title: Graves disease
entries.text: Graves disease The most common cause of hyperthyroidism; classically affects younger women. Hyperthyroidism is not the same word as thyrotoxicosis Thyrotoxicosis is excess thyroid hormone from any cause — including a gland that is leaking preformed hormone, or hormone somebody swallowed. Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid gland itself is overproducing. Every thyroiditis on this page causes thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism, which is exactly why their iodine uptake is low. Mechanism Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) , also called TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies, bind and activate the TSH receptor. The result is continuous, unregulated stimulation — so the gland both enlarges diffusely and overproduces. An antibody is doing the job TSH normally does, and no feedback loop can switch it off. Diagnosis ↑free T4, ↑free T3 or T3, ↓TSH. Antibodies: TSI or TSH-receptor antibody , plus anti-TPO and anti-TG. Imaging: radioactive iodine (I-123 / I-131) uptake scan . Three radioactive iodine uptake patterns Diffuse increased uptake across the whole gland indicates Graves disease. A single focal area of increased uptake with the rest of the gland suppressed indicates a hyperfunctioning nodule. Absent uptake indicates thyroiditis, where preformed hormone is leaking from a damaged gland that is not making new hormone. Diffuse uptake = Graves disease whole gland stimulated Focal uptake = hyperfunctioning nodule rest of gland suppressed No uptake = thyroiditis leaking, not making Original diagram — the uptake scan is the test that separates the three causes of a thyrotoxic patient. The logic is worth saying out loud: uptake measures whether the gland is making hormone . A thyroiditis is releasing hormone it made earlier, so it takes up nothing. Signs and symptoms The hypermetabolic, adrenergically amplified picture: weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations and tachycardia, tremor, anxiety and irritability, insomnia, frequent bowel movements, proximal muscle weakness, and menstrual irregularity. On examination, a diffuse goiter , a stare or lid lag, and warm moist skin. Two findings are specific to Graves rather than to thyrotoxicosis generally: Graves ophthalmopathy with exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema . Treatment Medical: methimazole, propylthiouracil (PTU), and beta blockers for symptom control. Definitive: surgery or I-131 radioactive iodine ablation . Details in the pharmacology section .

entries.title: Neonatal Graves & storm
entries.text: Neonatal Graves disease and thyroid storm Two high-acuity presentations that follow directly from Graves pathophysiology. Neonatal Graves disease maternal antibodies cross the placenta High acuity Mechanism Transplacental transfer of maternal TSH-receptor antibodies. The infant's own thyroid is normal — it is simply being stimulated by an antibody that crossed over. Almost always transient , resolving as the maternal antibody clears. The trap that kills Fetal thyrotoxicosis is possible in any mother with a history of Graves disease, regardless of her current thyroid status or treatment . TSI persists even after maternal thyroidectomy or radioablation — the gland is gone, the antibody is not. A euthyroid post-thyroidectomy mother is not a reassuring history. Symptoms Tachycardia · cardiomegaly and heart failure · irritability and restlessness · small for gestational age · prematurity · microcephaly · hepatosplenomegaly · stare or exophthalmos , from increased sympathetic stimulation of levator palpebrae superioris. Evaluation and treatment ↓TSH, ↑T4 and T3. Check thyroid antibodies in both infant and mother — TSH-receptor antibody and TSI. Treat with a beta blocker , PTU or methimazole , and iodine solution , for 2–4 months — until the circulating maternal antibodies resolve. Thyroid storm extremely rare, potentially fatal Emergency The pattern to recognize Occurs in untreated or undertreated hyperthyroidism, typically with a precipitating event such as surgery or infection . It is a hypermetabolic state: fever, tachycardia, nausea and vomiting, agitation, psychosis — progressing in the late stage to stupor, coma, and hypotension . The transition from agitated and hypertensive to obtunded and hypotensive is the ominous one. The reason a stressor precipitates it is worth holding: surgery or sepsis triggers a surge of catecholamines onto tissue that thyroid hormone has already made hypersensitive to them. That is also why a beta blocker is central to management.

entries.title: The thyroiditides
entries.text: Thyroiditis — telling the four apart Named individually in the course objectives. The comparative detail below is drawn from open-access references and cited. Two questions separate almost all of these at the bedside: does it hurt? and what is the uptake? Type Pain Hormone course RAI uptake Signature Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) Painful, tender gland Transient thyrotoxic → hypothyroid → usually recovers Low Follows a viral illness; raised inflammatory markers. The pain is what makes this one recognizable on a stem. Subacute lymphocytic (includes postpartum thyroiditis) Painless Transient thyrotoxic → hypothyroid → usually recovers Low Autoimmune, classically postpartum . Same triphasic course as de Quervain, without the pain. Hashimoto (chronic lymphocytic) Usually painless Often euthyroid, sometimes a brief thyrotoxic phase (hashitoxicosis), then permanent hypothyroidism Variable Anti-TPO and anti-TG positive , firm goiter. The one that does not recover. Riedel thyroiditis Usually painless Variable; hypothyroid if enough gland is replaced Variable Rare. A rock-hard, woody, fixed gland from dense fibrosis that extends into surrounding neck structures . Mimics anaplastic carcinoma — and that is the differential that matters. Why the uptake is low in the subacute forms Damaged follicles leak preformed hormone , producing low uptake; antithyroid drugs do not help because new hormone is not being synthesized.

entries.title: Goiter, cysts, sick euthyroid
entries.text: Goiter, thyroglossal duct cyst, and nonthyroidal illness Diffuse and multinodular goiter A goiter is simply an enlarged thyroid gland , and it reflects impaired thyroid hormone synthesis : output falls, TSH rises, and the rise in TSH drives hypertrophy and hyperplasia . Simple (diffuse) non-toxic goiter includes endemic goiter. Multinodular toxic goiter arises from recurrent cycles of hyperplasia and involution , producing irregular enlargement — and is often mistaken for neoplasia , which is precisely the reason it is worth knowing. Thyroglossal duct cyst A fibrous cyst forming from a persistent thyroglossal duct — the tract the thyroid descended along during embryogenesis. Presents in the midline, anterior to the trachea . The cyst pockets fill with clear secretions and mucus, and enlarge when infected , which is often when they are noticed. Midline is the discriminator: a lateral neck mass is a different differential. Nonthyroidal illness syndrome — also called sick euthyroid syndrome Abnormal thyroid laboratory values in a patient who is systemically ill but does not have primary thyroid disease . The classic picture is a low T3 with a normal-to-low TSH and a normal-to-low T4. Do not chase the numbers: treat the underlying illness and, if needed, re-test once the patient has recovered. Diagnosing and treating "hypothyroidism" in an intensive care unit on the strength of these values is the error the concept exists to prevent.

entries.title: Nodules and carcinomas
entries.text: Thyroid nodules and the four carcinomas Know the characteristic pathology and associations of each major type. Risk factors and presentation Risk: female preponderance · radiation exposure to the head and neck · exposure to radiation fallout · history of goiter · family history of thyroid cancer. Presentation: a neck mass, sometimes rapidly enlarging , with dysphagia, hoarseness, cough, or enlarged lymph nodes. Hoarseness deserves particular attention — it implies recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement. Know these four cold. Their relative frequency and signature findings answer most stems. Type Frequency Signature The point to carry Papillary Most common Empty nuclei devoid of nucleoli — "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei — and psammoma bodies Excellent prognosis. Commonly seen after prior ionizing radiation exposure. Treated with surgical excision, with or without radioactive iodine ablation. Follicular Second most common Invasion through the capsule is what defines malignancy Multinodular goiter may predispose; increased incidence in iodine-deficient regions . Appears as a cold nodule . Treatment is surgical excision. Medullary Uncommon Calcitonin secretion — it is a neuroendocrine neoplasm arising from parafollicular C cells Mostly sporadic, but hereditary disease is autosomal dominant via RET protooncogene mutations in MEN 2A and 2B . Treated by surgical excision of thyroid and lymph nodes — radiation and chemotherapy work poorly . Anaplastic Rare p53 point mutation of the tumor suppressor gene Highly aggressive and lethal. Affects an older population . Local invasion and metastasis are common at presentation — which is why it presents as a hard, fixed, rapidly enlarging mass with compressive symptoms. MEN syndromes — the medullary carcinoma link MEN 2A = medullary carcinoma + hyperparathyroidism + pheochromocytoma. MEN 2B = medullary carcinoma + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus. Both are autosomal dominant and both run through RET . The clinically urgent implication: screen for pheochromocytoma before operating on the thyroid, because an unrecognized pheochromocytoma makes anaesthesia dangerous. Follicular adenoma versus follicular carcinoma Two lesions with identical follicular architecture. In the adenoma the capsule is intact all the way around. In the carcinoma tumor tissue breaches the capsule. Because the deciding feature is at the capsule rather than within the cells, a fine-needle aspiration that samples only cells cannot distinguish them, and excision is needed. Follicular adenoma capsule intact all the way round benign Follicular carcinoma tumor breaches the capsule malignant Original diagram. The cells look the same in both — architecture cannot separate them. Capsular, and often vascular, invasion is the deciding histologic feature , and it lives at the edge of the lesion. That single anatomical fact is why fine-needle aspiration cytology frequently cannot call a follicular lesion, and why excision is often required. entries.title: When to biopsy
entries.text: Nodule evaluation — when tissue is needed The features that raise concern A firm, fixed, or rapidly enlarging nodule — particularly with a radiation history — is a nodule that needs fine-needle aspiration . An uptake scan characterizes function , not cytology, so it does not answer the malignancy question. A cold nodule is the one that raises concern. And a follicular lesion is the recognized exception where FNA may be insufficient and excision is required, because the diagnosis rests on capsular invasion. The order that makes sense 1. Check the TSH — this is cheap and it changes the path. 2. If the TSH is suppressed , the nodule may be autonomously functioning, so an uptake scan comes next; a hot nodule is very unlikely to be malignant. 3. If the TSH is normal or high, function is not the issue and the question is structural — ultrasound , and FNA of anything with concerning features. Follicular lesions require excision because malignancy depends on capsular or vascular invasion, which FNA cannot assess. Act The four drugs and drug classes named in this session

entries.title: Thyroid pharmacology
entries.text: Thyroid medications Levothyroxine synthetic T4 Hypothyroidism Use All causes of hypothyroidism, congenital and acquired. Given as tablets, titrated against the TSH in primary disease. Excess looks like hyperthyroidism Tachycardia, angina, tremor, insomnia, heat intolerance, weight loss — iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis. Labs show a suppressed TSH with a high free T4 and, importantly, a low or absent radioactive iodine uptake , because the exogenous hormone suppresses the gland. Distinguish from Surreptitious or excessive levothyroxine versus Graves disease: both give a high free T4 and a suppressed TSH. The uptake scan separates them — diffusely increased in Graves, low or absent with exogenous hormone — and a Graves patient has a goiter and possibly eye disease, which an exogenous-hormone patient does not. Thyroglobulin also falls with exogenous hormone, since the gland is switched off. Methimazole and propylthiouracil (PTU) antithyroid drugs Hyperthyroidism Mechanism Both block thyroid hormone synthesis . This is why they help in Graves disease, where the gland is overproducing, and why they are useless in a thyroiditis, where a damaged gland is leaking hormone it made earlier. Which one, when Methimazole is the preferred antithyroid drug in general use. PTU is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy , where methimazole carries a higher risk of congenital anomalies. PTU's own risk Hepatotoxicity, including hepatic failure. This is the trade-off for its safer first-trimester profile, and the reason PTU is not simply used for everyone. The shared serious risk: agranulocytosis Both drugs can cause agranulocytosis . Presentation is fever, severe sore throat, and oral ulceration — the classic teaching is that any patient on an antithyroid drug who develops fever and a sore throat needs an urgent white cell count , not reassurance. Shared trait Both cross the placenta, so either can cause transient neonatal hypothyroidism regardless of which is chosen. Radioactive iodine (I-131) and beta blockers definitive ablation · symptom control Definitive / symptomatic I-131 ablation Definitive treatment for Graves hyperthyroidism. It works by being concentrated in the very cells that are overactive. The expected consequence is worth stating plainly: it trades hyperthyroidism for lifelong levothyroxine-dependent hypothyroidism . That is a successful outcome, not a complication. Beta blockers — propranolol Control the adrenergic symptoms — tachycardia, tremor, anxiety — that thyroid hormone amplifies by increasing catecholamine sensitivity. Useful as a bridge while definitive treatment takes effect, and central to thyroid storm management. They do nothing to the underlying hormone excess. Retrieve Practice before you leave the page

entries.title: The chain
entries.text: Insulin, glucagon, and the consequence of absolute deficiency Glucose homeostasis is a balance of power between insulin , the anabolic storage signal, and glucagon and the other counter-regulatory hormones, which mobilize fuel. Insulin is the only hormone that lowers glucose; several act to raise it. Lose insulin entirely and the balance does not merely tilt — one side of it disappears, and the body behaves as though it is starving in the presence of abundant fuel. The metabolic consequences of absolute insulin deficiency Absolute insulin deficiency has four simultaneous effects. Muscle and fat take up less glucose. The liver increases glucose output through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Fat breaks down, releasing free fatty acids that the liver converts to ketones, causing an anion gap acidosis. Protein breaks down, supplying gluconeogenic substrate and causing weight loss and muscle wasting. The first two produce hyperglycemia, which exceeds the renal threshold and causes an osmotic diuresis, leading to polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, and electrolyte loss. No insulin action absolute deficiency ↓ glucose uptake muscle and fat cannot let it in ↑ hepatic output glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis Proteolysis muscle breaks down → amino acids Lipolysis fat breaks down → free fatty acids Hyperglycemia glucose piles up in the blood Ketogenesis liver turns FFA into ketone bodies Exceeds the renal threshold glucose spills into the urine Ketones are acids anion-gap metabolic acidosis Osmotic diuresis polyuria · polydipsia dehydration · electrolyte loss Diabetic ketoacidosis dehydration + acidosis together the emergency this all leads to Original diagram. Notice that the classic triad falls straight out of it: polyuria from the osmotic diuresis, polydipsia from the resulting dehydration, and polyphagia with weight loss from cells that cannot access glucose while fat and protein are being dismantled. Weight loss despite eating more is not a paradox — it is the whole mechanism in one sign.

entries.title: Forms of diabetes
entries.text: The forms of diabetes mellitus Worth learning before T1DM itself, because distinguishing T1DM from these other forms is largely a process of exclusion. "Diabetes" is a description of a glucose level, not a diagnosis — the diagnosis is which of these it is. Form Defining feature Key details T1DM Autoimmune beta-cell destruction → absolute insulin deficiency Primarily an immune-system disease occurring in genetically susceptible people after some environmental trigger. T2DM Insulin resistance with relative deficiency Covered in full on the T2DM page . Monogenic — MODY Single-gene defect in beta-cell function Mutations in enzymes and in insulin and beta-cell transcription factors. Monogenic and typically dominant . Often identified in adolescence or young adulthood. Neonatal diabetes Onset in the first month of life Definition: blood glucose above 120 mg/dL , occurring in the first month of life, lasting at least two weeks, requiring insulin. Transient or permanent. Monogenic — chromosome 6, IPF-1, glucokinase. Gestational diabetes First recognized in pregnancy Risk is higher with obesity and family history. Tested at 24–28 weeks , then again at 6–12 weeks postpartum . Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes Pancreatic damage from cystic fibrosis Grouped with chronic pancreatitis under "other specific types" in the standard classification. Medication or treatment induced A drug is doing it Chemotherapy — L-asparaginase, cyclosporine, tacrolimus — by direct beta-cell toxicity, interference with insulin secretion, or induced resistance. Atypical antipsychotics and anti-seizure medications. Glucocorticoids increase insulin resistance and drive gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown. American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care. 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27–S49. doi:10.2337/dc26-S002 Why gestational diabetes matters after the pregnancy ends For the mother: gestational diabetes signals a substantial future risk of T2DM — which is why the 6-to-12-week postpartum test exists and why it should not be skipped. For the child: prematurity, birth defects, neonatal hypoglycemia, being large for gestational age , and metabolic syndrome in adolescence . One pregnancy generates two long-term risk trajectories. Recognize Why it happens, how it presents, and what the labs show

entries.title: Autoimmune destruction
entries.text: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction The three-part formula worth memorizing Genetically susceptible individuals + an environmental trigger = an immune-system disease that destroys beta cells. Note the emphasis: this is primarily an immune-system disease that happens to be diagnosed by a glucose level. On histology, a normal islet gives way to insulitis — and the alpha and delta cells are preserved while the beta cells are picked off. The selectivity is the point: this is a targeted immune attack, not general pancreatic damage. The timeline of beta-cell loss before symptoms appear A timeline running left to right. Genetic susceptibility is present from birth. An environmental trigger initiates autoimmunity, at which point autoantibodies become detectable while beta-cell mass is still nearly normal and glucose is normal. Beta-cell mass then declines progressively over months to years, still without symptoms, because the remaining beta cells compensate. Symptoms appear abruptly only once the remaining beta-cell mass can no longer meet demand. A partial recovery known as the honeymoon phase may follow the start of treatment, before beta-cell loss completes. Time — months to years, not to scale beta-cell mass glucose trigger autoimmunity begins autoantibodies detectable here symptoms SILENT PHASE — OFTEN YEARS ABRUPT birth Original schematic; axes are relative and unscaled. The clinically important shape: the autoimmune process runs silently long before anything is noticeable , because the surviving beta cells compensate. Glucose only rises — and then rises fast — once that reserve is exhausted. This is why a child can appear entirely well one month and present in ketoacidosis the next, and why autoantibodies can be positive years before diagnosis . Genetic risk The strongest named genetic associations are HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 , which affect antigen presentation to T cells. Proposed environmental triggers Viral and other environmental exposures may contribute, but no single trigger is established.

entries.title: Clinical presentation
entries.text: Clinical presentation The three Ps Polyuria — glucose exceeds the renal threshold and drags water with it. Polydipsia — thirst chasing that fluid loss. Polyphagia — hunger, because the cells cannot access the fuel circulating past them. In children, add nocturia and new nocturnal enuresis : a previously dry child wetting the bed again is a classic and easily dismissed presentation. What makes it T1DM rather than T2DM on the history Weight loss despite increased appetite , over weeks rather than years, in someone without an insulin-resistance phenotype. Loose clothing and a tightened belt are the details students overlook. A short, catabolic history points to absolute deficiency; an incidental A1c in someone with obesity points elsewhere.

entries.title: Diagnostic criteria
entries.text: Diagnosing and classifying with laboratory data Applies to T1DM and T2DM alike. Standard diagnostic thresholds, with the conventional threshold phrasing alongside. Test Normal Prediabetes / impaired glucose tolerance Diabetes Fasting plasma glucose Below 100 mg/dL 100–125 mg/dL >125 mg/dL (conventionally written ≥126) 2-hour glucose on OGTT Below 140 mg/dL 140–199 mg/dL >199 mg/dL (conventionally ≥200) HbA1c Below 5.7% 5.7–6.4% >6.4% (conventionally ≥6.5%) Random plasma glucose — — >199 mg/dL with symptoms The confirmation rule that questions are built on Asymptomatic patients require two abnormal results, on subsequent days, to confirm the diagnosis. A single abnormal value in someone with no symptoms is not a diagnosis. The exception is the symptomatic patient with a random glucose above 199 — there, symptoms plus the value are enough, and the reason is obvious once you think about it: someone with classic symptoms and a glucose of 350 does not need a repeat test tomorrow, they need treatment today. American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care. 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27–S49. doi:10.2337/dc26-S002 Autoantibodies — is it autoimmune? GAD-65 , ICA-512 (IA-2) , and insulin autoantibodies (IAA) . Their presence supports T1DM. Note the direction of the inference: they identify the mechanism , not the severity. C-peptide — is there any endogenous insulin? C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin in a one-to-one ratio with insulin , so it measures what the pancreas is making. Low in T1DM (the beta cells are gone) and normal or high in T2DM (they are working hard against resistance). Critically, C-peptide is not present in injected insulin — so it is also the test that distinguishes endogenous hyperinsulinism from someone who has taken insulin. Retrieve A patient has documented hypoglycemia with a high insulin level. How does C-peptide tell you whether the insulin came from their pancreas or a syringe? The pancreas makes proinsulin and cleaves it into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts , so anything the pancreas secretes raises both together. Manufactured insulin contains no C-peptide. So: high insulin with high C-peptide = endogenous overproduction — an insulinoma, or a drug that pushes the beta cell to secrete, such as a sulfonylurea. High insulin with suppressed C-peptide = the insulin came from outside the body. The same logic makes C-peptide a marker of residual beta-cell function when classifying diabetes. Localize Deciding which form of diabetes you are looking at

entries.title: T1DM vs everything else
entries.text: Distinguishing T1DM from T2DM, monogenic, and secondary diabetes Features used to classify diabetes Starting from confirmed hyperglycemia, four groups of evidence are weighed. Islet autoantibodies and a low C-peptide point to T1DM. An insulin-resistance phenotype with negative antibodies and a preserved or high C-peptide points to T2DM. Onset in the first month of life points to neonatal diabetes; dominant inheritance across generations without autoimmunity or resistance points to MODY. Cystic fibrosis, pancreatic disease, or a causative medication points to secondary diabetes. No branch is decisive on its own. Confirmed hyperglycemia now: which form? Autoimmunity? GAD-65 ICA-512 (IA-2) IAA C-peptide low? Resistance? Acanthosis nigricans Obesity C-peptide high? Age & family? First month of life? Neonatal. Dominant across 3 generations? MODY Context? Cystic fibrosis Pancreatitis Steroids or tacrolimus antipsychotics READ ALL FOUR — NONE OF THEM IS DECISIVE ALONE · People with T2DM can present in ketoacidosis. · People with T1DM can have obesity — the two coexist. · MODY is routinely misclassified as T1DM or T2DM for years. · A negative antibody panel does not by itself exclude T1DM. Treat each feature as evidence to be weighed, never as proof. Original diagram. The framework is deliberately not drawn as a strict decision tree with single yes/no gates, because the real reasoning weighs the branches together. Act Management principles, the acute complications, and DKA

entries.title: Management and acute complications
entries.text: Management, and the acute complications short of DKA Management combines lifelong insulin, glucose monitoring, carbohydrate-based dosing, education, and psychosocial support . The non-negotiable principle T1DM requires insulin at all times — including when the patient is not eating, and including when they are unwell and eating nothing at all. Basal insulin is not "the insulin for food." Stopping it because someone is not eating is how a person ends up in ketoacidosis, because without any insulin the liver resumes ketogenesis regardless of intake. Hypoglycemia Why it is the limiting problem Autonomic warning symptoms — sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety — normally give a person time to act. Hypoglycemia unawareness removes that warning, so the first sign becomes a neuroglycopenic one: altered mental status or seizures . Someone with unawareness is not less sick; they are less protected. A pharmacology point worth carrying Non-selective beta blockers blunt the adrenergic warning symptoms — the tremor and palpitations in particular — producing a drug-induced version of unawareness. Sweating is largely cholinergically mediated and tends to persist , which is why it is the symptom to ask about specifically in a patient on a beta blocker. Morning hyperglycemia — two mechanisms with different fixes Both produce a high morning glucose, and the correct responses point in opposite directions — which is exactly why the distinction is taught. Dawn phenomenon Somogyi effect Mechanism Morning hyperglycemia caused by counter-regulatory hormones — GH and cortisol — as part of their normal secretion Morning hyperglycemia caused by rebound from an early-morning hypoglycemia , through the counter-regulatory response to that low Overnight glucose Drifts up, or stays steady, then rises toward morning Dips low in the early hours, then rebounds How you tell Check a glucose in the early hours of the morning. There is no way to distinguish them from the morning value alone. Memory hook Normal hormones, ordinary timing SOMogyi = SO MUCH INSULIN causing the overnight low Retrieve Someone wakes with a glucose of 260 every day and wants to increase their bedtime basal insulin. What do you need to know first, and why does it matter so much? What the glucose did overnight — specifically, a reading in the early hours of the morning. If the overnight trace ran steady or drifted upward, the morning high reflects the dawn phenomenon , and more overnight insulin is a reasonable direction. If the trace dipped low before rebounding, this is the Somogyi pattern, and increasing the evening dose would deepen a nocturnal hypoglycemia that is already happening while the patient is asleep and unable to notice it. The two look identical at 7 a.m. and call for opposite actions — which is the entire reason the pair is taught together.

entries.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis
entries.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis The acute complication the objectives ask you to explain mechanistically, recognize on labs, and manage in principle. Scope, before we start DKA is due to lack of insulin and is usually a feature of T1DM — but patients with T2DM can present with DKA too. Do not treat DKA as diagnostic of T1DM, and do not treat the presence of T2DM as reassurance against it. The DKA causal cascade Insulin deficiency splits into two arms. On one arm, hyperglycemia exceeds the renal threshold and causes an osmotic diuresis, which produces dehydration and washes potassium out of the body, depleting total body stores. On the other arm, lipolysis releases free fatty acids that the liver converts into ketone bodies, which are acids, producing an anion gap metabolic acidosis; the body compensates with deep rapid Kussmaul breathing that lowers arterial carbon dioxide. Both arms converge on diabetic ketoacidosis. Meanwhile acidosis and insulin deficiency drive potassium out of cells into the blood, so the measured serum potassium may be normal or high even though total body potassium is severely depleted. Insulin deficiency Hyperglycemia (typically >250) Osmotic diuresis Dehydration + urinary loss of potassium Lipolysis → free fatty acids Liver makes ketone bodies Anion-gap metabolic acidosis → Kussmaul breathing lowers PaCO₂ Diabetic ketoacidosis RUNNING UNDERNEATH BOTH ARMS · THE POTASSIUM PARADOX Acidosis and insulin deficiency push potassium OUT of cells, so the measured serum potassium can look normal or high while total body potassium is severely depleted. Original diagram of the underlying mechanism: absence of intracellular insulin alters lipid metabolism, free fatty acids are shunted into ketone body formation, and ketones are acids — hence ketoacidosis. Laboratory findings and physical signs Diagnostic laboratory thresholds Glucose typically above 250 mg/dL. Bicarbonate below 15 mEq/L. Increased anion gap, typically above 16. Ketones present in blood and urine. Physical findings Dehydration · Kussmaul respirations · a fruity odor on the breath from ketonemia · non-focal abdominal tenderness · nausea and vomiting · altered mental status. The abdominal pain is worth flagging — DKA is a well-known mimic of a surgical abdomen, and the pain typically resolves as the acidosis does. The potassium paradox Total-body potassium is depleted by osmotic diuresis, even when serum potassium appears normal or high because insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells. Insulin drives potassium back into cells , so monitor closely and replace potassium during treatment. Glaser N, Fritsch M, Priyambada L, et al. ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Pediatr Diabetes. 2022;23(7):835–856. doi:10.1111/pedi.13406 Management principles Course principles only; clinical treatment follows an institutional protocol. Fluid first. These patients are volume depleted from the osmotic diuresis. Restoring circulating volume improves perfusion and, on its own, begins to lower the glucose by improving renal clearance of it. Insulin, to switch off ketogenesis. The purpose of the insulin is not primarily to lower the glucose — it is to stop lipolysis and ketone production and close the acidosis. This is why insulin continues even once the glucose has come down, with glucose added to the fluids to permit that. Potassium, anticipated rather than reacted to. See the paradox above. The expected fall is planned for. Monitor closely — glucose, electrolytes, acid–base status, and mental status. The anion gap closing is the marker that the underlying process is resolving; the glucose normalizing is not. Find and treat the precipitant. Infection, missed insulin, an interrupted pump, or a new diagnosis. A DKA that is treated without the trigger being identified tends to recur.
