entries.title: The progression
entries.text: Insulin resistance, compensation, and beta-cell failure Insulin resistance Target tissues — muscle, fat, liver — respond poorly to insulin. Glucose is not taken up efficiently and the liver does not suppress its output as it should. Nothing is wrong with the beta cell yet. Compensatory hyperinsulinemia The beta cell answers resistance by secreting more insulin , and for a long while it succeeds: glucose stays normal at the cost of a rising insulin level. This is why a normal glucose does not mean a normal metabolism — and why C-peptide is high, not low , in T2DM. Beta-cell dysfunction The compensation is not sustainable. Secretory capacity declines, and the gap between what is needed and what is delivered opens. Insulin deficiency in T2DM is relative , not absolute — which is exactly why ketoacidosis is uncommon here and hyperosmolar states are not. Worsening hyperglycemia Glucose crosses the prediabetes range, then the diabetes threshold. By this point the process has been running for years — which is why microvascular complications are sometimes already present at the moment of diagnosis, and why screening at-risk people rather than waiting for symptoms matters so much. Genetics and environment T2DM has a strong genetic contribution , expressed through interaction with nutrition, activity, sleep, and other environmental factors. Recognize Who to suspect, what to look for, and what the labs show

entries.title: Suspicion and signs
entries.text: Clinical suspicion and physical findings Symptoms Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia — the same three Ps, because the mechanism downstream of the hyperglycemia is identical. Plus nocturia and nocturnal enuresis . The difference from T1DM is tempo : this often accumulates so gradually that the patient does not report it, and the diagnosis comes from a screening test rather than a complaint. Signs and history Acanthosis nigricans · overweight or obesity · family history , which carries particular weight given how strong the heritability is here. Look at the back of the neck and the axillae on anybody you are screening. Acanthosis nigricans — what it actually is Velvety, thickened, hyperpigmented skin in flexural areas: the back and sides of the neck, the axillae, the groin, sometimes the knuckles. It is not a hygiene problem and does not scrub off — a distinction worth making explicitly, because patients are frequently told otherwise. It is a visible marker of insulin resistance , and a recognized clinical sign of both prediabetes and T2DM. Finding it on examination should prompt a glucose or A1c, not reassurance. Hughes EK, Brady MF, Rawla P. Acanthosis Nigricans. StatPearls [Internet]. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431057

entries.title: Screening and diagnosis
entries.text: Screening, prediabetes, and the diagnostic thresholds Diagnostic thresholds for prediabetes and diabetes Three tests shown as bands. Fasting plasma glucose: normal below 100, prediabetes 100 to 125, diabetes above 125 milligrams per deciliter. Two-hour glucose on an oral glucose tolerance test: normal below 140, prediabetes 140 to 199, diabetes above 199. HbA1c: normal below 5.7 percent, prediabetes 5.7 to 6.4 percent, diabetes above 6.4 percent. A random plasma glucose above 199 with symptoms is also diagnostic. Asymptomatic patients require two abnormal results on subsequent days. NORMAL · PREDIABETES · DIABETES Fasting plasma glucose (mg/dL) < 100 100 – 125 > 125 2-hour glucose on OGTT (mg/dL) < 140 140 – 199 > 199 HbA1c (%) < 5.7 5.7 – 6.4 > 6.4 TWO MORE RULES THAT QUESTIONS ARE BUILT ON · A random glucose > 199 mg/dL WITH SYMPTOMS is diagnostic on its own. · Asymptomatic patients need TWO abnormal results on subsequent days. Original figure. The conventional written forms of the same cut-points are fasting ≥126 mg/dL, 2-hour ≥200 mg/dL, and A1c ≥6.5% — the strict-inequality phrasing above describes the same boundaries. Bar widths are for legibility and are not to scale. Prediabetes / impaired glucose tolerance Defined by the middle band on all three tests. Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical sign at this stage too, and treatment is nutrition and exercise , with medication therapy as an option. The framing that matters: prediabetes is not a mild version of diabetes, it is a point on the curve where the trajectory can still be changed . Labs that support T2DM specifically Negative GAD-65 antibody, islet cell antibody, and insulin autoantibody. Elevated C-peptide and insulin. Read together: no autoimmunity, and plenty of endogenous insulin being made — the problem is that it is not working. Compare with T1DM , where C-peptide is low. American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care. 2026;49(Suppl 1):S27–S49. doi:10.2337/dc26-S002 T1DM versus T2DM — the comparison the objectives ask for explicitly. Every row is a tendency, not a rule; see the classification exercise on the T1DM page . T1DM T2DM Core defect Autoimmune beta-cell destruction → absolute insulin deficiency Insulin resistance → beta-cell dysfunction → relative deficiency Autoantibodies Positive — GAD-65, ICA-512, IAA Negative C-peptide Low Normal or elevated Body habitus Often lean, with recent weight loss — but obesity does not exclude it Usually overweight or obesity, with central adiposity Acanthosis nigricans Not characteristic Characteristic Onset Weeks — catabolic, symptomatic, sometimes in DKA Years — often silent, often found on screening Family history May be present, but is less characteristic A close relative with diabetes is common Characteristic emergency DKA HHS — but neither is exclusive to one type Insulin required Always, from diagnosis, permanently Sometimes, and often later in the disease

entries.title: Metabolic syndrome
entries.text: Metabolic syndrome Also called insulin resistance syndrome, or syndrome X — named in Gerald Reaven's 1988 Banting Lecture as a cluster of effects downstream of hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance. Metabolic syndrome as a hub around insulin resistance Abdominal obesity drives insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia, which sits at the center. Radiating from it are central adiposity, raised blood pressure, high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, and hyperglycemia. Adipocyte cytokines feed back into the center. All of these converge on the ultimate threat, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Abdominal obesity BMI and weight are not the criterion Insulin resistance = hyperinsulinemia Central adiposity cytokines ↑ Blood pressure hypertension ↑ Trigly- cerides dyslipidemia ↓ HDL cholesterol dyslipidemia Hyper- glycemia → T2DM Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease the "ultimate threat" of the cluster THE DEADLY QUARTET Abdominal obesity · hyperglycemia · dyslipidemia (high TG, low HDL) · hypertension Original diagram of the pathway Reaven's framework describes. Note the causal direction: abdominal obesity drives insulin resistance , resistance produces hyperinsulinemia, and the cluster of features radiates from there rather than merely co-occurring. Reaven GM. Banting Lecture 1988. Role of insulin resistance in human disease. Diabetes. 1988;37(12):1595–1607. doi:10.2337/diab.37.12.1595 What insulin resistance produces Impaired peripheral glucose and fatty acid utilization · vascular endothelial dysfunction · impaired lipid metabolism · hypertension . Note that endothelial dysfunction appears here, at the metabolic-syndrome stage — before diabetes is diagnosed. The vascular disease does not wait for the glucose threshold. The detail that catches people Explicitly: BMI and weight are not a criterion — it is abdominal obesity that matters. Someone with a BMI in the normal range but central adiposity can meet the definition, and someone with a high BMI and a favorable fat distribution may not. The comorbidities that travel with T2DM Hypertension · dyslipidemia · fatty liver disease · chronic kidney disease · polycystic ovary syndrome · obstructive sleep apnea · hyperuricemia and gout · metabolic syndrome. Most share insulin resistance as a common root, which is why they cluster. Localize Separating the two hyperglycemic emergencies

entries.title: HHS, and HHS vs DKA
entries.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, and how it differs from DKA Diagnostic features Hyperglycemia — glucose above 600 mg/dL. Hyperosmolality — serum osmolality above 330 mOsm/kg. No acidosis , and the absence of significant ketosis . Those three together define it. Kitabchi AE, Umpierrez GE, Miles JM, Fisher JN. Hyperglycemic crises in adult patients with diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2009;32(7):1335–1343. doi:10.2337/dc09-9032 Why there are no ketones — the mechanistic heart of the topic HHS arises from relative insulin deficiency, with a rise in counter-regulatory hormones because glucose is not being used, and increased hepatic and renal glucose production through gluconeogenesis . The idea is worth memorizing almost verbatim: there is just enough circulating insulin to prevent lipolysis and the subsequent free fatty acid production, but not enough insulin to support adequate glucose utilization . Say it as a threshold problem Suppressing lipolysis takes less insulin than driving glucose into cells does. So as insulin availability falls, glucose uptake fails first while lipolysis stays switched off. The patient becomes profoundly hyperglycemic without making ketones. Only when insulin falls further — as in T1DM — does lipolysis get released and ketogenesis begin. One axis, two thresholds : that single idea explains why DKA and HHS are different presentations of the same hormone deficit, and why the type of diabetes predicts which one you tend to see without determining it. DKA versus HHS. Read the "insulin available" row first — every other difference follows from it. Feature DKA HHS Insulin available Essentially absent — absolute deficiency Present but insufficient — relative deficiency Degree of hyperglycemia Typically above 250 mg/dL — high, but usually less extreme Above 600 mg/dL — far higher Ketones Present , and central to the diagnosis Absent or insignificant Acidosis Anion-gap metabolic acidosis ; bicarbonate below 15, anion gap typically above 16 No acidosis Serum osmolality Raised Above 330 mOsm/kg — this is the defining derangement Dehydration Marked Profound — the osmotic diuresis has run for longer at a higher glucose Neurologic manifestations Altered mental status, usually tracking the acidosis Prominent — altered mental status tracking the osmolality, and often the presenting problem Breathing Kussmaul respirations , compensating for the acidosis Not a feature — there is no acidosis to compensate for Typically associated with T1DM T2DM, often an older patient Speed of onset Hours to a couple of days Days to weeks Neither emergency is exclusive to one type of diabetes Patients with T2DM can present with DKA , and older adults with T1DM can develop HHS. The associations in the last two rows above are typical , not defining. Diagnose the emergency from the glucose, the ketones, the acid–base status, and the osmolality — never from the label already in the chart. HHS complications Thrombosis — profound dehydration and hyperviscosity · rhabdomyolysis , and through it acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and hypocalcemia, which together can cause cardiac arrest · muscle swelling leading to compartment syndrome · malignant hyperthermia · cerebral edema . entries.title: Treatment approaches
entries.text: Treatment The point of this section is that there are many treatment modalities — the emphasis is on the categories and the lifestyle foundation, not on individual drug pharmacology. Nutrition and dietary counseling Weight stabilization , then weight loss — a widely used initial target is 7% of body weight · eliminate sugary beverages · encourage plant-based eating · and, importantly, identify the patient's dietary preferences . Named patterns: Mediterranean, low calorie, low fat, DASH, intermittent fasting. Medical nutrition therapy centers on no concentrated sugars and carbohydrate monitoring , with support from family, friends, school, and work. Exercise counseling Children: 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic activity per day. Adults: 150 minutes per week. Muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on 3 days per week for both. Screen-time counseling belongs alongside these, particularly for children and adolescents. Glucose monitoring Patient-specific. Options: fasting, pre-meal, and 2-hour post-prandial checks; standard basal-bolus monitoring at 4 times daily ; or continuous glucose monitoring . Medication categories Four broad modalities: oral medication , insulin therapy , oral medication plus insulin , and injectable glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. Insulin in T2DM is a tool used when the others are insufficient, not a sign of failure — a framing worth passing on to patients. American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care. 2026;49(Suppl 1). diabetesjournals.org/care/issue/49/Supplement_1 A scope note on pharmacology This page stays at the level of treatment categories . It does not work through the mechanisms, adverse effects, or comparative benefits of individual agents — metformin, sulfonylureas, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, and the rest. Coursework cases mention specific drugs by name, so recognizing which category a named drug belongs to is reasonable to expect; detailed pharmacology is not covered here and this page does not manufacture it. One safety-relevant point does belong here , because it appears in the practice bank: among oral agents, the insulin secretagogues — the sulfonylureas, such as glipizide, glyburide, and glimepiride — can cause hypoglycemia , particularly when meals are missed or delayed, whereas metformin used alone does not.

entries.title: Chronic complications
entries.text: How chronic hyperglycemia damages tissue From chronic hyperglycemia to organ complications Chronic hyperglycemia acts through three mechanisms: advanced glycation end-products formed by non-enzymatic glycation, sorbitol accumulation via aldose reductase, and oxidative stress with inflammation. These converge on two vascular pathways. Microvascular injury produces retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. Endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis produce coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral arterial disease. Chronic hyperglycemia AGEs non-enzymatic glycation alters protein structure → permeability, stiffness, cytokines, ischemia Sorbitol accumulation aldose reductase makes it; no sorbitol dehydrogenase to clear it → osmotic and oxidative injury Oxidative stress and inflammation amplifies both of the other two pathways Microvascular injury small vessels, capillaries, nerves Endothelial dysfunction → accelerated atherosclerosis MICROVASCULAR · Retinopathy · Nephropathy · Neuropathy "the three -opathies" MACROVASCULAR · Coronary artery disease · Cerebrovascular disease · Peripheral arterial disease occlusion, thrombosis, gangrene Extent is determined by DURATION of diabetes and DEGREE of glucose control. Those are the two levers — one you cannot change, one you can. Original diagram tracing the standard damage mechanisms through to the named complications. Microvascular complications Retinopathy Retinal ischemia and neovascularization ; fragile new vessels can bleed and threaten vision. Nephropathy Albuminuria/proteinuria from glomerular injury; control glucose and blood pressure and screen for early disease. Neuropathy Sorbitol accumulation and AGE injury damage peripheral nerves and Schwann cells. Macrovascular complications Coronary artery, cerebrovascular, and peripheral arterial disease from endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis. entries.title: Basal versus bolus
entries.text: What insulin therapy is trying to reproduce Basal insulin restrains hepatic glucose output between meals and overnight; bolus insulin covers meals. Every regimen attempts to reproduce both jobs. A basal-bolus day Across a 24-hour day, a low continuous basal insulin level covers overnight and between-meal periods. Three carbohydrate loads at breakfast, lunch, and dinner each produce a rise in glucose demand, matched by a mealtime bolus given at each meal. A separate correction dose can be added to a mealtime bolus, or given on its own between meals, to bring an out-of-range glucose back toward target. BASAL — continuous background, overnight and between meals breakfast lunch dinner CARBOHYDRATE LOAD BOLUS — one per meal, sized to the carbohydrate CORRECTION — added to a meal bolus, or given alone 12a 8a 1p 6p 12a Two jobs, two kinds of insulin. A regimen that cannot separate them has to constrain the patient's day instead. When a glucose pattern is abnormal, identify which insulin was acting beforehand. The rule underneath everything T1DM requires insulin at all times, with no exceptions for illness or reduced intake. Basal insulin is not "the insulin for food," and it is not paused because someone is not eating. Without any insulin at all, the liver resumes ketogenesis regardless of what the patient has or has not eaten. Recognize The five categories, and what each one's shape means clinically

entries.title: Insulin action curves
entries.text: Insulin profiles Know the categories and the examples within each. The curves let you see why the category matters clinically, not just as a label. Rapid-acting Lispro (Humalog), aspart (NovoLog), glulisine (Apidra). On and off quickly, with an early peak — which is what lets it match a meal and then get out of the way. It is also the only insulin used in a pump. Regular — short-acting Regular human insulin (R). Slower on, and it lasts longer than the meal does. That tail is the reason regimens using regular insulin traditionally require timed snacks: the insulin outlives the food. NPH — intermediate NPH (N). A broad mid-range peak. That peak is both its usefulness — it can cover a meal several hours after injection — and its hazard, because a peak that arrives while the patient is asleep is a peak nobody is watching. Long-acting and ultra-long-acting Glargine (Lantus), detemir (Levemir) — relatively flat across roughly a day. Degludec (Tresiba) — essentially peakless and lasting beyond 24 hours, so doses overlap between days and a change takes several days to show its full effect. Flatness is the feature: a basal insulin is meant to have no peak to fall off. Premixed 70/30 and 75/25. A fixed ratio of an intermediate component and a rapid or short-acting component in one injection. Fewer injections, but the ratio is fixed — you cannot adjust the meal coverage without also moving the background insulin. That single constraint drives most of the trade-offs in the regimen table below. A practical bedside detail worth knowing cold NPH is cloudy. Regular and rapid-acting insulins are clear. It is a bedside safety check that costs nothing: if a vial that should be clear is cloudy, or a patient describes drawing up the wrong appearance, something has gone wrong before the injection. Thota S, Akbar A. Insulin. StatPearls [Internet]. Treasure Island (FL): StatPearls Publishing. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560688 Classify The four regimens, and what each one costs the patient

entries.title: Regimen comparison
entries.text: The four commonly used regimens Every regimen buys something and pays for it somewhere else. The "major vulnerability" column is where the exam questions live. Regimen What it is Flexibility Meal timing Dose burden Major vulnerability Correct hyperglycemia? MDI / basal-bolus 1–2 basal injections (glargine, detemir, degludec) plus 2 or more mealtime injections (lispro, aspart, glulisine) High — carbohydrate amount is flexible Meal timing variable; basal needs consistent timing More than 4 injections daily ; snacks not required but may need their own insulin Number of injections, and the discipline it asks for Yes — even when not eating Pump / CSII Continuous basal infusion plus 2 or more boluses. Rapid-acting analog only. Highest — basal rates vary through the day; temporary basal rates for acute changes Fully flexible "One injection" every 3 days; worn 24 hours a day, brief disconnection allowed Technology fails. No long-acting depot, so an interruption becomes ketosis within hours. Higher expense. Yes , and most precisely — dosing in 0.025–0.05 unit increments Twice-daily (BID) 2 injections of intermediate insulin (NPH) mixed with rapid-acting or regular Low — a set amount of carbohydrate per meal Strict times for meals and injections; snacks must be eaten with the insulin peaks Fewer injections per day — this is the trade being made Activity and day-to-day variability make it hard; a peak arriving when food does not causes hypoglycemia Less likely Premixed 2 or more injections of 70/30 or 75/25 Lowest — the ratio of the two components is fixed Strict, as for BID Fewest decisions; simplest to teach You cannot move one component without moving the other Least likely of all — the fixed ratio makes an isolated correction the hardest to deliver of any regimen here Why the pump is described as the most physiological It is the only regimen that can change the basal rate by time of day — more insulin in the pre-dawn hours when counter-regulatory hormones are rising, less during an afternoon of exercise. A basal injection commits you to one profile for the whole 24 hours. Temporary basal rates allow acute adjustments for illness or activity, and the fine dosing increments make ratios and correction factors usable in a way pens cannot match. Why the pump's failure mode is the sharpest A pump contains rapid-acting insulin only . There is no long-acting depot underneath it. When delivery stops — occluded set, dislodged cannula, empty reservoir — the patient's entire insulin supply stops within a couple of hours, and ketosis follows quickly. This is why unexplained hyperglycemia on a pump prompts a check of the delivery system before any thought of adjusting doses. Donner T, Sarkar S. Insulin — Pharmacology, Therapeutic Regimens and Principles of Intensive Insulin Therapy. Endotext [Internet]. South Dartmouth (MA): MDText.com. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK278938 Act The arithmetic, and then the pattern reading

entries.title: ICR, correction, target
entries.text: The three numbers a patient carries Insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (ICR) The insulin required to cover the breakdown of carbohydrate into sugars and keep glucose in target. Written as "1 unit per XX grams." A larger XX is a weaker ratio. Correction factor (sensitivity factor) The insulin required to bring an out-of-range glucose down to target. Written as "1 unit decreases glucose by XX mg/dL." Basal insulin / basal rate, and target The insulin required to hold glucose at target when fasting or not eating . The target glucose is the number the correction aims at — corrections are calculated from the distance above it, which is why two patients with the same glucose can need different corrections. Retrieve Two patients both read 240 mg/dL. One has a correction factor of 1 unit per 25 mg/dL, the other 1 unit per 80. What does that difference tell you about them — before you calculate anything? The patient whose correction factor is 1 unit per 80 mg/dL is far more sensitive to insulin — a single unit moves their glucose a long way, so they need very few units to correct. The patient at 1 unit per 25 is much more insulin-resistant; each unit accomplishes less, so they need several times as many units for the same correction.

entries.title: Glucose pattern lab
entries.text: Glucose pattern lab The one principle this whole section teaches Evaluate the insulin that acted before the repeated abnormal pattern. Two words in that sentence do a lot of work. "Before" — you work backwards from the abnormal reading to whatever insulin was acting during the hours leading up to it, which is often not the insulin given nearest in time. "Repeated" — one bad day is a missed dose or an unusual meal, not a pattern. Confirm it repeats across several days before attributing it to an insulin period at all. Working the same logic on a twice-daily NPH regimen The reasoning is identical, but the answers change because the insulin shapes change. Read this table off the action curves rather than memorizing it — NPH given in the morning peaks in the afternoon, so it is the insulin covering the pre-dinner reading, and NPH given in the evening peaks overnight, so it is the insulin covering the fasting reading. Twice-daily NPH mixed with rapid-acting or regular insulin. This is an application of the action curves, not a separate rule to memorize. Glucose reading that is repeatedly abnormal Which insulin was acting before it Why Fasting / pre-breakfast Evening NPH Its broad peak falls across the overnight hours Pre-lunch Morning rapid-acting or regular The mealtime component given with breakfast covers the late morning Pre-dinner Morning NPH Injected at breakfast, it peaks through the afternoon Bedtime Evening rapid-acting or regular The mealtime component given with dinner covers the evening Why this table is a hazard as well as a tool Look at the fasting row. On a twice-daily regimen, a high fasting glucose points to the evening NPH — but so does an overnight low , because it is the same insulin peaking at the same hour. Raising the evening NPH to fix a morning high, without first checking what happened at three in the morning, is precisely the error the dawn phenomenon versus Somogyi distinction exists to prevent.

entries.title: Regimen cases
entries.text: Cases — reasoning across regimens Original cases written to cover the regimen types above. Each opens to a worked answer. Case 1 — MDI, morning highs Basal-bolus A college student with T1DM takes a long-acting basal insulin each morning, with an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 unit per 4 g and a correction factor of 1 unit per 20 mg/dL above 120. They report consistent morning highs and want to increase the basal dose. What do you want to know, and what is the risk of simply agreeing? Work it through Reveal the reasoning Ask what the glucose does overnight — the pattern between bedtime and waking, over several days. A steady drift upward supports increasing the basal. A dip in the early hours followed by a rebound means more basal would deepen a nocturnal hypoglycemia. Then notice the timing. The basal is taken in the morning . Long-acting analogs are relatively flat but not perfectly so, and their weakest coverage tends to fall at the far end of the dosing interval — which here is the overnight period. So the question is not only how much basal but when it is given. And check the bedtime bolus. A very strong ratio of 1 unit per 4 g means a large evening dose, and insulin still active from it changes the overnight picture. Look at the whole night before touching a standing dose. Case 2 — premixed insulin and a mid-afternoon low Premixed A young adult with long-standing T1DM has switched from MDI to a premixed 70/30 regimen, taking a larger morning dose and a smaller evening dose, because the injection burden had become unmanageable. They now report lows in the mid-afternoon and highs before bed. What is happening, and what does the regimen make difficult? Work it through Reveal the reasoning The mid-afternoon low is the intermediate component of the morning injection peaking — a large morning dose means a large afternoon peak, arriving whether or not the patient eats. This is the reason twice-daily regimens require snacks timed to the insulin peaks . The pre-bed high is the evening injection's rapid component being too small for the evening meal. The bind: the 70/30 ratio is fixed. Reducing the morning dose to fix the afternoon low also reduces the morning meal coverage. Increasing the evening dose to cover dinner also increases the overnight intermediate component. You cannot move one component without moving the other — which is the trade the patient accepted in exchange for fewer injections. Recognizing that the regimen, not the patient, is generating the pattern is the clinical point. Case 3 — pump user, A1c rising after a job change CSII An adult with T1DM on pump therapy with continuous glucose monitoring has held an A1c below 7.0% for years. It has risen to 8.1% since starting a new job. The pump is functioning and sets are being changed on schedule. Where do you look? Work it through Reveal the reasoning At the pattern, by time of day, and specifically at whether boluses are being given at all. A pump's great advantage — that a bolus is a few button presses rather than an injection — is also the easiest thing to postpone during a busy day and then forget. Missed or late mealtime boluses are among the most common reasons an established pump user's control drifts, and the bolus history in the pump answers the question directly. Then ask what else changed with the job: meal timing, meal content, activity level, sleep, and stress. A regimen that worked for one daily rhythm may need different basal rates for a different one — which the pump can accommodate, once you know which hours are the problem. Note what this case is not : the sets are being changed and the pump works, so this is not a delivery failure. Delivery failure looks like the pump-interruption trace in the pattern lab — a rapid, unrelenting rise over hours, not a gradual drift in A1c over months. Case 4 — hypoglycemia unawareness Safety An older adult with long-standing T1DM and known hypoglycemia unawareness is on a twice-daily NPH and regular regimen. Why

entries.title: Look-alike pairs
entries.text: Pairs that get confused Each of these is a pair where the wrong answer is the other member of the pair. Learn the discriminator, not the pair. Pair The discriminator Hyperthyroidism vs thyrotoxicosis Thyrotoxicosis is excess hormone from any source; hyperthyroidism means the gland is overproducing . A thyroiditis causes the first without the second. Graves disease vs exogenous thyroid hormone Uptake scan — diffusely increased vs absent. Graves also has a goiter and may have eye disease. Subacute granulomatous vs subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis Pain. Granulomatous (de Quervain) hurts; lymphocytic does not, and is classically postpartum. Riedel thyroiditis vs anaplastic carcinoma Both are hard, fixed masses in an older patient. Tissue diagnosis — you cannot settle it clinically, and one is lethal. Follicular adenoma vs follicular carcinoma Capsular invasion , which sits at the edge of the lesion — so FNA often cannot call it and excision is needed. Papillary vs follicular carcinoma on FNA Papillary has nuclear features — Orphan Annie eye nuclei, psammoma bodies — so cytology works. Follicular does not. Sheehan syndrome vs pituitary apoplexy Speed and mechanism. Sheehan is postpartum ischemic necrosis presenting insidiously; apoplexy is acute hemorrhage into an adenoma with a thunderclap headache. Prolactinoma vs stalk effect Magnitude. Prolactin correlates with adenoma size, so a very high prolactin favors a prolactinoma; a moderate rise beside a non-prolactin-secreting mass is stalk effect. Craniopharyngioma vs Rathke cleft cyst Both from Rathke pouch. The cyst is benign and often incidental; the craniopharyngioma grows , compresses the chiasm, and causes hypopituitarism. Gigantism vs acromegaly Epiphyseal plates. Open → gigantism; closed → acromegaly. Same hormone, same tumor. AVP deficiency vs AVP resistance The response to desmopressin. Clinically identical otherwise. Bitemporal vs homonymous hemianopsia Where the lesion sits relative to the chiasm. At it → bitemporal. Behind it → homonymous. In front of it → one eye only. Dawn phenomenon vs Somogyi effect The overnight glucose. Drifting up vs dipping low then rebounding. The morning value looks identical. DKA vs HHS How much insulin is left. None → lipolysis and ketones. A little → enough to suppress lipolysis, not enough for glucose uptake. T1DM vs T2DM Antibodies plus C-peptide , read alongside phenotype, age, and family history. No single feature is decisive. Cushing disease vs Nelson syndrome Whether cortisol is high. Nelson follows adrenalectomy — very high ACTH with hyperpigmentation and mass effect, but no hypercortisolism.

entries.title: Insulin
entries.text: Insulin — profiles, regimens, and the three numbers Three tables cover the whole Insulin Therapy 101 objective set. Worked examples are on the insulin lab . Action profiles Toggle these as overlapping curves on the action-curve figure . Category Examples Onset Peak Duration Rapid-acting lispro, aspart, glulisine ~15 min ~1–2 h 2–4 h Regular (short) regular human insulin (R) ~30–60 min ~2–4 h 6–8 h Intermediate NPH (N) ~1–2 h broad, ~4–8 h 12–16 h Long-acting (basal) glargine, detemir ~1–2 h relatively flat glargine ~24 h; detemir ~20–24 h, dose-dependent Ultra-long-acting degludec ~1 h essentially peakless >24 h — doses carry over between days Premixed 70/30, 75/25 two components: an early rapid/short peak, then a later NPH peak ~10–16 h Bedside shorthand from the lecture: NPH is "cloudy," regular and rapid-acting are "clear." The four regimens, and the trade-off in each Compared side by side on the regimen comparison . Regimen What it is Pro Con Basal-bolus (MDI) 1–2 basal plus 2+ mealtime injections — glargine/detemir/degludec with lispro/aspart/glulisine Flexible carbs and meal timing; can correct a high even when not eating More than 4 injections a day; basal needs consistent timing Pump (CSII) Continuous basal infusion plus boluses — rapid-acting only Most physiologic; basal adjustable through the day and by temp basal; dosing to 0.025–0.05 units; one site change every 3 days Worn 24 h; technology fails; expensive. No depot — a failure means ketosis within hours Twice daily (BID) 2 intermediate injections mixed with rapid or short — NPH plus lispro/aspart/glulisine or regular Fewer injections Set carbs per meal, strict meal and injection timing, must eat snacks to cover the peaks ; poorly suited to variable activity Premixed 2+ injections of 70/30 or 75/25 Fewest decisions All of the BID limitations, plus it is the least able to correct a hyperglycemia — the ratio is fixed The three numbers Know what each one means ; the formulas were flagged as optional. Practice on the dose exercises . Term The question it answers Read as Insulin-to-carb ratio (ICR) How much insulin covers the carbohydrate about to be eaten 1 unit per XX grams of carbs. A smaller XX means more insulin per gram. ICR = 540/TDD Correction / sensitivity factor How much insulin brings a high glucose back to target 1 unit drops glucose by XX mg/dL . A smaller XX means more insulin per point. CF = 1800/TDD (or 1500) Basal insulin / basal rate How much insulin holds glucose steady while fasting Judged by the overnight and between-meal trend, not by post-meal numbers. T1DM needs insulin at all times. For adjusting a regimen, the whole principle is one sentence — see the pattern-management prompt below.

entries.title: Must-not-miss
entries.text: The time-sensitive presentations What each one looks like, and the single feature that should make you act. Emergency Setting The finding that should move you Pituitary apoplexy Known or silent pituitary adenoma Sudden excruciating headache with visual change — and cardiovascular collapse , which is acute cortisol deficiency. A true neurosurgical emergency. Thyroid storm Untreated or undertreated hyperthyroidism, after a stressor such as surgery or infection Fever with marked tachycardia and agitation. Progression to stupor and hypotension is the ominous turn. Neonatal Graves disease Infant of a mother with Graves disease — regardless of her current thyroid status Tachycardia and irritability in the first days; high acuity if unrecognized. DKA Usually T1DM — but T2DM can present this way Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, dehydration, with an anion-gap acidosis. Watch the potassium and watch for cerebral edema . Cerebral edema in DKA During DKA treatment, especially age under 5 Altered or fluctuating consciousness, headache, emesis — and the counter-intuitive pair: falling heart rate with rising diastolic pressure . Mannitol or 3% saline. HHS Usually T2DM, often an older patient Glucose above 600, osmolality above 330, no acidosis and no ketones , with prominent neurologic change. Severe hypoglycemia Anyone on insulin or an insulin secretagogue Altered mental status or seizure. In hypoglycemia unawareness this is the first sign, not a late one. Severe hyponatremia in SIADH Small-cell lung cancer, CNS disease, drugs Confusion or seizure with a low sodium and a concentrated urine. No peripheral edema. Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis Anyone on methimazole or PTU Fever with severe sore throat and oral ulceration. Needs an urgent white cell count, not reassurance. Pump delivery failure Insulin pump user A rapid, unrelenting glucose rise over hours. Rapid-acting insulin only, no depot — ketosis follows quickly.

entries.title: Complications & metabolic syndrome
entries.text: Chronic complications and metabolic syndrome The diagram version of the damage pathway is on the T2DM page . Metabolic syndrome — the "deadly quartet" Also called insulin resistance syndrome or syndrome X (Reaven, 1988). Worked through on the T2DM page . The four The detail that gets tested Abdominal obesity BMI and total weight are not the criterion — the fat distribution is. Hyperglycemia The consequence of insulin resistance, not the starting point. Dyslipidemia Specifically high triglycerides and low HDL . Hypertension One of several downstream effects of endothelial dysfunction. Chain to carry: abdominal obesity → insulin resistance → hyperinsulinemia and adipocyte cytokines → impaired glucose and fatty-acid use, vascular endothelial dysfunction , impaired lipid metabolism, hypertension. The ultimate threat is atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease , not the glucose. How hyperglycemia does the damage Three mechanisms, converging on two vascular pathways. Mechanism What happens Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) Non-enzymatic glycation alters protein structure and function → increased vascular permeability, arterial stiffness, cytokines → inflammation and tissue ischemia. Sorbitol accumulation Aldose reductase makes it; there is no sorbitol dehydrogenase to clear it → osmotic and oxidative injury. Oxidative stress and inflammation Amplifies the other two rather than acting alone. Microvascular versus macrovascular Know which bucket each belongs to — that alone answers most stems. Complication The point to carry Microvascular small vessels, nerves Retinopathy Driven by ischemia and neovascularization . Accelerated by longer duration after puberty, worse control, hypertension, smoking, pregnancy. Nephropathy Characterized by protein in the urine . Early detection allows intervention; ACE inhibitor , blood-pressure and glucose control, no smoking. Neuropathy Sorbitol injury via aldose reductase plus AGE damage to myelinated nerves and Schwann cells. Conduction changes after ~4–5 years. Macrovascular endothelial dysfunction → accelerated atherosclerosis Coronary artery disease Cardiovascular disease is ~70% of morbidity and mortality in diabetes — the leading cause, and the reason the macrovascular bucket matters more than its three-item length suggests. Cerebrovascular disease Peripheral artery disease Two variables govern all of it: duration of diabetes and degree of glucose control . The DCCT is the evidence — intensive control produced a 60% reduction in the development and progression of complications. Treatment modalities The objective asks you to know that there are many modalities, not to pick between agents. Modality Specifics named in the lecture Nutrition Weight stabilization then 7% weight loss ; eliminate sugary beverages; plant-forward; match to preference — Mediterranean, low-calorie, low-fat, DASH, intermittent fasting. Exercise Children 60 min/day moderate-to-vigorous; adults 150 min/week , plus strengthening 3 days/week. Glucose monitoring Fasting, pre-meal, 2-hour post-prandial; 4× daily on basal-bolus; or CGM. Medication Oral (e.g. metformin), insulin, oral plus insulin, or injectable glucose-lowering agents.

entries.title: One-line mechanisms
entries.text: Mechanisms in one line each Finding Mechanism Goiter Impaired hormone synthesis → TSH rises → hypertrophy and hyperplasia. Adrenergic look of hyperthyroidism Thyroid hormone increases catecholamine sensitivity — hence the tremor, tachycardia, and the usefulness of a beta blocker. Absent uptake in thyroiditis Preformed hormone is leaking from damaged follicles; no new synthesis, so no iodine trapping. Bitemporal hemianopsia Temporal field → nasal retina → fibers cross in the middle of the chiasm → a mass pushing up from the sella hits them first. Stalk effect on prolactin Prolactin is under tonic dopamine inhibition ; interrupt the stalk and the brake comes off. Hyperpigmentation in Nelson syndrome Adrenalectomy removes cortisol feedback → ACTH rises enormously → pigmentary effects. Sheehan syndrome The pituitary enlarges in pregnancy while its blood supply does not; peripartum hemorrhage tips it into infarction. Failure to suppress GH after oral glucose Hyperglycemia normally suppresses GH; an autonomous somatotroph adenoma ignores it. GH rise on the insulin tolerance test Hypoglycemia is a physiological stimulus to GH; failure to rise defines the deficiency. No peripheral edema in SIADH Water is retained but blood volume stays normal, so it distributes rather than pooling in the interstitium. Weight loss with polyphagia Cells cannot access glucose, so fat and protein are dismantled for fuel while the patient keeps eating. Kussmaul respirations Respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis — deep, rapid breathing drives PaCO₂ down . Potassium paradox in DKA Acidosis and insulin deficiency push K⁺ out of cells, so serum K⁺ looks normal or high while total body K⁺ is depleted. Insulin then drops it fast. No ketones in HHS Suppressing lipolysis takes less insulin than driving glucose into cells; enough remains for the first job, not the second. Acanthosis nigricans A visible cutaneous marker of insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia. Diabetic neuropathy Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, which cannot be cleared → osmotic and oxidative injury; AGEs damage myelinated nerves and Schwann cells. Proliferative retinopathy Ischemia drives neovascularization; the new vessels are fragile and bleed. Complications present at diagnosis of T2DM Glucose is the last variable to move — resistance and beta-cell decline preceded it by years. Missed hypoglycemia on a beta blocker Adrenergic warning symptoms are blunted; sweating is cholinergic and tends to persist. Ketosis within hours of a pump failure A pump holds rapid-acting insulin only — there is no long-acting depot to buy time.

entries.title: Rapid recall prompts
entries.text: Rapid recall prompts Answer out loud before opening any of these. Retrieve Name the four anterior pituitary hormones in the order they are typically lost, and say which one is the dangerous one and why. GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH. ACTH is the dangerous one: it is lost last , so it is easy to miss, and cortisol deficiency is what kills under the stress of illness or surgery. GH going first is useful in the other direction — its loss foreshadows the deficits still to come. See hypopituitarism . Retrieve Why does a thyroiditis cause thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism, and what does that mean for treatment? Damaged follicles release hormone they made earlier . The gland is not synthesizing, so the uptake scan is blank and antithyroid drugs — which block synthesis — have nothing to act on. Symptom control with a beta blocker while it runs its course is the logical approach. See the thyroiditides . Retrieve A patient in DKA has a serum potassium of 5.2. Describe their total body potassium, and what happens after you start insulin. Total body potassium is severely depleted — hours to days of osmotic diuresis, plus vomiting, have been washing it out. The serum value looks reassuring only because acidosis and insulin deficiency have shifted potassium out of cells into the compartment you are sampling. Start insulin and potassium moves back into cells; correcting the acidosis does the same. The serum concentration can fall quickly , unmasking the deficit. Hence close monitoring and anticipatory replacement. See DKA . Retrieve State the pattern-management principle in one sentence, and name the two words in it that do the work. "Evaluate the insulin that acted before the repeated abnormal pattern." Before — work backwards from the abnormal reading to whichever insulin was acting in the hours leading up to it, which is frequently not the dose given nearest in time. Repeated — a single bad day is a missed bolus or an unusual meal, not a pattern, and changing a standing dose on the strength of it causes hypoglycemia on all the normal days. Practice it in the pattern lab . Retrieve Give the one-sentence reason DKA makes ketones and HHS does not. Suppressing lipolysis requires less insulin than driving glucose into cells does. In HHS there is just enough insulin to keep lipolysis switched off but not enough to support glucose utilization, so the glucose climbs enormously without ketones. In DKA insulin is essentially absent, lipolysis is released, and the liver converts the resulting free fatty acids into ketone bodies. One axis, two thresholds. See HHS versus DKA . Retrieve A patient has polyuria, hypernatremia, and very dilute urine. Walk through the two steps that get you to a diagnosis. Step 1 — water deprivation. Ask whether they can concentrate their urine when dehydration should be a maximal stimulus to do so. Continuing to pass high volumes of dilute urine despite dehydration confirms an AVP disorder, without yet saying which. Step 2 — give desmopressin. Now ask whether the hormone is missing or the kidney is deaf to it. Urine osmolality rises substantially → AVP deficiency (the kidney was competent, just unsupplied). Little or no rise → AVP resistance (the kidney cannot respond to hormone it is definitely now receiving). Serum AVP answers the same question from the other side: low in deficiency, normal or high in resistance. Work it interactively at the desmopressin figure . Go to cumulative practice →
